before._label: Original APS (double-bend achromat, 1995-2023), as last operated before the April 2023 shutdown

beamCurrent.note: Timing mode (48 bunches) is limited by injector charge: 130 mA / 140 mA.

rfFrequency.source: fdr2 Table 2.48 (342 ppm above the old ring, fdr2 Table 2.3)

emittanceAt200mA.source: upd202504 ('emittance is even smaller than our previous world record: 33 picometers radians')
emittanceAt200mA.note: Coupling mode and ID-gap state not stated - treat as approximate.

rfVoltage.value: 4.5 typical; up to 6.5 with all ID gaps closed
rfVoltage.source: srp2024 ('nominal voltage of 4.5 MV total, going up to 6.5 MV when all gaps are closed'); fdr2 Table 2.42: 6.43 MV max

rfCavities.unit: single-cell copper 352-MHz cavities, 4 per straight in 3 straights (sectors 36, 37, 40)
rfCavities.source: srp2024; fdr2 2-3.10; fdr5 (the 12 cavities in sectors 36, 37, 40 were kept in place; sector-38 cavities removed)

rfPowerSources.value: two 1-MW klystrons in operation (four 1-MW stations RF1-RF4 for the ring + RF5 for the booster); transition to solid-state amplifiers began 2026 (first sector = 4 cavities), full ring expected by 2028

beamLifetime.source: ler25 slide 20 ('Lifetime 2 - 4 hours'); design 10th-percentile: 2.91 h (48 b) / 5.96 h (324 b) fdr2 Table 2.45; 3.7-15 h fdr2 Table 2.13
beamLifetime.note: Lifetime is shorter than design; momentum acceptance lower than expected (ler25 slide 14).

storedBeamEnergy.source: fdr2 Table 2.45 (derived check: 6 GV x 736 nC = 4.42 kJ)

value.source: ipac25 (130 mA), napac25 and ler25 (140 mA)

value.mode: standard lattice 'typically 162 singlets or greater' + timing-mode blocks

bunchModesAsOperated.note: The 324-bunch design brightness mode has not been reported in user operation; 216-bunch spacing = 6 rf buckets = 17.0 ns (derived).

vacuumChamber.value: mostly NEG-coated round chambers, 22 mm diameter (11 mm inner radius, 1 mm wall); NEG-coated water-cooled copper in the high-power FODO bends; extruded aluminium with antechamber in the M1/M2 L-bends; Inconel at the fast correctors

vacuumConditioning.value: design 0.01 nTorr/mA after 1000 A-h was reached after only ~300 A-h

orbitStabilityRequirement.value: AC (0.01-1000 Hz): 1.3 um / 0.25 urad (H), 0.4 um / 0.17 urad (V); 7-day drift 1.0 um / 0.6 urad (H), 1.0 um / 0.5 urad (V)

orbitStabilityAsBuilt.value: Fast orbit feedback (22 kHz update, 1 kHz bandwidth) was descoped from the project; uncorrected motion is close to spec; 1-Hz then 50-Hz workstation correction with 240 correctors; residual 30-Hz line from a FODO-module rocking mode (simulated at 40 Hz); FOFB being completed in operations (single-sector test first)

userHoursPerYear.value: 5000 typical; 4896 planned for FY2026 to allow extra machine studies

bmSourceSizes.unit: um rms / urad rms (electron beam at the nominal BM source point, zero current)
bmSourceSizes.note: Added by verifier: electron-beam size at the bending-magnet (B:M3) source point, for the BM-beamline hotspots.

type.value: hybrid seven-bend achromat (H7BA, ESRF-EBS concept) with six additional reverse bends per sector

dipolesPerSector.value: 13 = 7 main bends (4 longitudinal-gradient M1/M2 + 3 transverse-gradient M3/M4) + 6 reverse bends (Q4, Q5, Q8; offset quadrupoles)

magnetsPerSector.unit: lattice magnets per sector (29 main magnets + 4 fast eight-pole correctors)
magnetsPerSector.source: fdr2 2-3.1 ('each sector contains 7 dipoles, 10 standard quadrupoles, 6 reverse bends, six sextupoles, and four fast steering correctors totalling 33 lattice magnets / sector'); fdr2 2-3.2 (29 main magnets)
magnetsPerSector.note: srp2024 (Borland, Aug. 2024) says 'eight ordinary quadrupoles' per sector; the FDR (2-3.1, 2-3.2, Table 2.5: Q1, Q2, Q3, Q6, Q7, two of each) and FDR Fig. 2.32 count 10, and the as-built total of 1,321 magnets matches the FDR tally of 33/sector. The srp2024 wording remains unexplained. Re-checked by verifier against fdr2 Table 2.5 and Fig. 2.32.

magnetsTotal.source: fdr2 2-3.1 ('33 lattice magnets / sector, or 1,321 magnets for the entire 40 sectors (one extra corrector is employed near the injection point)'); n20240420; n20260205; apsNSR
magnetsTotal.note: Resolved by verifier: 33 x 40 = 1,320 plus one extra corrector near the injection point = 1,321. The Aug. 2026 profile quoting '1,320' counts only the 40 identical sectors.

modules.unit: pre-assembled magnet modules (5 per sector: DLM-A, QMQ-A, FODO, QMQ-B, DLM-B)

magnetStrength.value: quadrupoles up to ~80-100 T/m (Q7 86 T/m, Q1 79 T/m), sextupoles up to ~5,000-6,800 T/m^2; vanadium-permendur pole tips; 13 mm minimum pole-tip radius
magnetStrength.source: fdr2 Tables 2.5-2.6 and 2-3.1; ipac21 ('order 100 T/m and 6800 T/m^2', 13-14 mm bores); apsNSR: magnets 'up to five times stronger' than the originals

reverseBends.value: Q4, Q5, Q8 are quadrupoles mounted off-axis so the beam also sees a weak dipole field bending the 'wrong' way (-0.07 to -0.31 deg each). The extra dipole 'knob' lets the designers shape the dispersion independently of the beta functions, lowering the natural emittance from 67 pm (same lattice without reverse bends) to 42 pm
reverseBends.source: fdr2 2-2.1 ('allowing reduction of the natural emittance to 42 pm compared to 67 pm in the design without reverse bends'; 'help manipulate the dispersion independently of the beta functions'), Table 2.4
reverseBends.note: fdr2 2-2.1.3: the weak dipole fields of Q4 and Q5 sit where the dispersion is large, so they are very effective at adjusting the damping partition and let the dispersion be raised in the sextupoles and brought back down in M2; without reverse bending there the minimum emittance would be 58 pm. Angles from fdr2 Table 2.4: Q4 -0.098 deg, Q5 -0.066 deg, Q8 -0.307 deg (verified).

totalBendingAngle.unit: degrees (sum of absolute bend angles; net 360)
totalBendingAngle.source: derived from fdr2 Table 2.4: +9.945 deg - 0.942 deg per sector x 40; ipac21 quotes 'from 360 to 435 degrees'

brightness.definition: Brightness (also 'brilliance') = photons per second per mm^2 of source area per mrad^2 of beam divergence in a 0.1% energy bandwidth. It measures how many photons come from how small a spot into how narrow a cone - what you need to focus x-rays to tiny spots or to do coherent experiments.

statements.text: The upgraded APS produces X-ray beams 'up to 500 times brighter' than the original APS.
statements.note: Facility headline number; the gain depends on photon energy and on which undulator is compared.

statements.text: At 20 keV, with an undulator optimized for 20 keV, brightness and coherent flux rise by a factor of about 540 (brightness mode 3.25e22 vs 6e19 ph/s/mm^2/mrad^2/0.1%BW).

Over a broad range of hard X-ray energies up to and beyond 100 keV the design gain is a factor of 100 to 1000; the project goal was at least two orders of magnitude for >20 keV, 10-100x more single-bunch brightness for timing experiments, and twice the average flux.
statements.source: fdr2 2-1.2; fdr1 1-2; ipac21 ('two to three orders of magnitude in the 10-100 keV range'; 'twice the spectral flux')

statements.text: The gain depends on photon energy: in the IPAC'21 design envelope it is roughly x200 at 10 keV, x700 at 20 keV and x600-800 at 50-100 keV for brightness, and roughly x160 at 10 keV and x600 at 20 keV for coherent flux.
statements.source: derived from digitized ipac21 Fig. 1 (see dataPoints, +/- ~20%)
statements.note: Reason: the old horizontal emittance (3.1 nm) was far above the photon 'diffraction limit' lambda/4pi at all hard-X-ray energies, so shrinking it helps most where lambda/4pi is smallest (high energy).

statements.text: Horizontal electron emittance fell from ~3,100 pm to ~42 pm (natural; 28-44 pm measured depending on coupling) - a factor of ~75, which APS rounds to 'almost a factor of 100'.
statements.source: sp2025 ('lowered by almost a factor of 100 to 40 pm.rad'); fdr2 Table 2.1; ipac25 Table 1

statements.text: World-record low emittance for a synchrotron light source at the time: 45 pm (flat beam, 50 mA) and 28 pm (round beam), vs 134 pm previous record at ESRF-EBS.
statements.note: 33 pm measured at 200 mA in April 2025. 'World record' refers to Aug. 2024. Check by verifier: China's HEPS (also 6 GeV, design ~35 pm) reported a measured 93 pm in January 2025, so no lower measured emittance than APS-U's was found as of Oct. 2026.

statements.text: More than 100-fold increase in coherent flux; 'over two orders of magnitude' increase in brightness and coherence.
Superconducting undulators, once installed, are expected to add about another factor 3 in brightness above 50 keV; the objective KPP brightness is expected to be exceeded 3-4x with in-line SCUs.
Approximate transverse coherent fraction (zero current, no energy spread, 2.4-m undulator): at 10 keV ~0.05% for the old APS vs ~3% (round) to ~6% (flat) for APS-U; at 20 keV ~0.015% vs ~1-3%.
statements.source: derived (formula in dataPoints 'coherentFractionEstimate'); consistent with beamline design values 4.2-5.6% at 10 keV and 0.5-0.9% at 25 keV (fdr4 Tables 4.41, 4.51)

statements.text: APS-U horizontal emittance is comparable to the photon emittance lambda/4pi at ~2-3.5 keV (42-29 pm); the flat-beam vertical emittance (~4 pm) matches lambda/4pi at ~25 keV. The old ring's 3.1 nm matched lambda/4pi only at ~30 eV.
No measured APS-U brightness curve has been published that we could find; all curves below are design calculations.
statements.source: search of APS news, JACoW 2024-2026, sp2025 (brightness KPP measurement was planned after SCU installation)

concept.value: On-axis 'swap-out' injection: instead of topping up stored bunches (accumulation), the weakest stored bunch is kicked out to a dump and replaced in the same rf bucket by a fresh, full-charge bunch from the injector - no accumulation needed, so the ring can work with a tiny dynamic aperture (~+/-1.5 mm).

worldFirst.value: APS-U is the first storage-ring light source to use (multi-bunch) swap-out injection; first multi-bunch swap-out on 2024-04-29 (12 bunches, 1.1 mA target, 30-s interval, 0.6 nC from the BTS)

plane.source: desy24; ler25; ipac21 ('injected horizontally on-axis using a pulsed 1.4-T septum magnet, 3 horizontal fast kickers')
plane.note: The 2019 FDR described vertical injection with a DC Lambertson septum and separate extraction kickers in the sector-38 straight (fdr2 2-2.8, 2-3.6). By 2021 the design had changed to horizontal injection with a pulsed septum; as built, the same three kickers inject the new bunch and kick the old one out.

septum.value: pulsed, single-turn, direct-drive septum magnet: 1.42 T peak over 1.493 m, blade tapering to 3 mm; 18 kA in a 1-mm copper bus
septum.source: napac25 ('a septum blade that tapers to 3 mm thickness at the downstream end'; 23 days, ~1 million pulses); ipac25; ler25 slides 26-27
septum.note: First septum failed after ~1 million pulses (23 days); the spare then leaked; the repaired original went back in. Its stored-beam tube was bowed so that it touched the design orbit ~0.7 m from the exit, so the magnet was pivoted about its exit (0.7 mrad per napac25/ipac25; 1.5 mrad per ler25 slide 27). The septum chamber was replaced by Oct. 2025 (ler25 slide 21) and a new septum design is being built (ler25 slide 27).

injectionKickers.value: 3 stripline kickers in one straight, horizontal, 3 mrad total, ~11 ns pulses (+/-~25 kV, 'about 27 kV' pulsers); allow filling every third rf bucket
injectionKickers.source: ler25 slide 5; desy24 slide 12; ipac21; harkay23; srp2024
injectionKickers.note: A 2024 APS all-hands slide reportedly lists 27-kV stripline pulsers with a 20-ns pulse (search-engine summary only, not opened); ler25 slide 5 and ipac21 give ~11-ns pulses. Treat 11 ns as the as-built kicker pulse length per the 2025 commissioning slides.

gapSeptumToKicker.unit: mm (horizontal gap between septum wall and first kicker blade)

emittanceExchange.value: 6 skew quadrupoles in the BTS swap the booster beam's large horizontal and small vertical emittances so it fits the 2.8-mm gap

decoherenceKicker.value: vertical, 0.2 mrad, 11 ns, fired 200-250 turns before injection to blow up the outgoing bunch and protect the swap-out dump (~100x lower particle density in design)
decoherenceKicker.source: ler25 slide 5 (200 turns); desy24 and napac25 (250 turns); fdr2 2-2.8.2
decoherenceKicker.note: The FDR (2-2.9) describes the same pre-kick idea for the superseded vertical scheme: a weak stripline 'pre-kicker' ~250 turns ahead reduces the energy density on the dump by two orders of magnitude.

fanOutKicker.value: vertical, 0.1 mrad, 5 us half-sine over a full turn; fires on a whole-beam abort to spread all bunches over the beam-dump surface

program.value: fills the requested pattern at 1 Hz, then swaps out the weakest bunch at the requested interval

replacementCriterion.value: design: a bunch is replaced when its charge has fallen to about 90% of nominal; in 2025 operation the weakest bunch is replaced on a fixed ~20-s clock, allowing larger drops (see sampleParameters216)

intervalDesign.value: about 25-30 s (48 bunches, 3.5-4 h lifetime) and 7.5-18 s (324 bunches)
intervalDesign.source: ipac21; fdr2 Table 2.13 (16-30 s round beam, 8-10 s flat 324-bunch)

intervalOperational.value: kept close to 20 s (200 mA, 216 bunches, Oct. 2025)
intervalOperational.source: ler25 slide 23 ('Keeping swap-out interval close to 20 seconds')
intervalOperational.note: With a ~2-h lifetime this means each bunch drops by roughly 40-50% before it is replaced, far more than the 10% assumed in the FDR; the resulting bunch-to-bunch charge non-uniformity is accepted.

sampleParameters216.source: ler25 slide 23 ('Sample swap-out parameters for 200 mA and 216 bunches'); column order (Drop % | BTS charge nC | Interval s) confirmed by verifier from the rendered slide image.

initialFill.value: each bunch first filled with slightly more than I_total/N_bunches = 3.4 nC (216 bunches)

injectionEfficiency.value: very good despite septum aperture limit; shot-to-shot variation < 1% rms over 2 months of user operation

electronsInjected.value: ~40x more electrons injected than with top-up at the old APS; ~90% of them end in the shielded swap-out dump
electronsInjected.note: Both numbers are FDR design values that assume bunches are replaced at ~90% of their charge. In 2025 operation bunches drop by ~40-50% before replacement (ler25 slide 23), so roughly half of the injected charge, not 90%, ends in the swap-out dump (derived by verifier).

injectorChargeNeeded.value: 17 nC (48 bunches) ... 2.5 nC (324 bunches) per shot at 200 mA

swapOut.figureNote: FDR Figs. 2.17-2.18 show the superseded 2019 vertical-injection layout; use them only as background.

dumpsAndCollimators.value: Design (FDR 2019): five horizontal whole-beam dumps/collimators (aluminium, nominal +/-4.8-mm aperture, just upstream of A:Q4 where horizontal beta and dispersion are largest) in sectors 37, 38, 39, 40 and 1, inside the thicker 'Zone F' tunnel shielding; their surfaces can be moved vertically to present a fresh surface after a dump, because a full 200-mA beam dumped in one spot 'will carve a groove in any kind of material'. A whole-beam dump is triggered by tripping the rf. The swap-out dump was a +/-4.58-mm vertical collimator inside the A:M1 magnet of sector 39 (vertical-injection design). As built (2025): collimators sit ~3 mm from the orbit rather than the expected ~4.5 mm, prioritising ID protection over lifetime; the fan-out kicker spreads the bunches over the dump surface during a full-beam abort.
dumpsAndCollimators.note: Added by verifier. The as-built location of the swap-out dump after the change to horizontal injection is not given in any source opened.

purpose.value: Passive 'bunch-lengthening system' (BLS): stretches each electron bunch so electrons collide less often inside the bunch (Touschek scattering), raising lifetime; also eases intrabeam scattering and rf heating of chamber parts

type.value: single-cell superconducting niobium cavity, TESLA cell shape, beam-driven (no external rf drive)

frequency.unit: MHz (4th harmonic of the 352-MHz main rf)
frequency.note: ipac24bls quotes the tuning reference as '1296 x beam revolution frequency or 1.408321 GHz'; 4 x 352.056 MHz (fdr2 Table 2.48) = 1408.22 MHz, so the last digits of that quote are inconsistent (likely a typo).

temperature.unit: K (superfluid helium via J-T valve inside the cryomodule)

cryomodule.value: 2-m cryomodule; with HOM absorbers and tapers occupies 2.4 m (just under half a ~5-m straight); the other half holds longitudinal-feedback kickers

value.tuner: pneumatic helium-bellows tuner (ATLAS heritage), ~600 kHz range

parameters.source: ipac24bls Table 1 and text (nominal values, 'final values TBD')

cryoPlant.value: dedicated Linde LR140 helium refrigerator, up to 2.5 g/s of 4.3-K liquid helium

lifetimeGain.value: about 2x measured (4x expected); lifetime 1.5 h at zero BLS voltage (100 mA, 162 bunches)

measuredProfile.value: double-peaked (over-stretched) bunch profile, peak ratio ~1.6:1, as predicted

history.value: installed before commissioning; tested at 0.5 MV with 50 mA (June 2024); first use with user beam Oct. 8 (2024, year inferred) at 0.5 MV after quench-interlock issues; 1.1 MV at 200 mA by 2025
history.source: desy24 slide 18; ler25 slide 18; sp2025 ('already operating')

designLifetimeTarget.value: ~3.5 h (48 bunches, 200 mA) vs ~1 h without the BLS

timeline.event: Electrons make their first turn around the original APS storage ring. On 25 March, the radio-frequency system first captures them in stable bunches.
The US Department of Energy approves the need for an APS upgrade. This is Critical Decision 0, or CD-0, the first formal approval for a major DOE project.

A July 2013 report by DOE's Basic Energy Sciences Advisory Committee recommends multi-bend-achromat rings. Around 2014, APS physicist Michael Borland outlines an initial APS design in technical note LS-337. The date is approximate.
timeline.source: ls337 (CVS revision dated March 5, 2014, per search-engine summary of the PDF; the PDF itself returned 403)

timeline.event: DOE approves the multi-bend-achromat design and the project's cost range under a revised Critical Decision 1, or CD-1.
DOE's Basic Energy Sciences Advisory Committee describes the upgrade as "absolutely central" and "ready to initiate construction".
DOE approves advance purchases of components with long manufacturing times. This is the CD-3B procurement approval.
DOE approves the project's scope, schedule and $815 million budget. This CD-2 approval establishes the performance baseline.
The project publishes the Final Design Report, APSU-2.01-RPT-003, detailing the new ring and beamlines.
DOE approves construction of the $815 million upgrade under CD-3.
The project has incurred half its planned cost. COVID-19 delays have moved expected first beam back ten months to mid-2024.
The original APS storage ring shuts down permanently. Experiments begin a planned period of about a year without X-rays.
Removal of the old storage ring is complete, 60 days after shutdown.
The first of 200 pre-assembled magnet modules is installed in the tunnel.
The linear accelerator restarts. The particle accumulator ring follows in October 2023 and the booster synchrotron in February 2024.
The first vacuum bake-out begins. Heating the chambers under vacuum removes gas from their walls.
The last of 200 magnet modules is installed, 162 days after the first.
The last component is installed, completing storage-ring assembly.
Testing and vacuum bake-out of the new ring are complete.
An Accelerator Readiness Review checks that the new accelerator can operate safely.
DOE authorizes commissioning. Operators can begin circulating beam and tuning the new ring.
Electrons make their first turns around the new ring.
timeline.note: upd202504 says electrons first circulated on April 14.

timeline.event: The ring stores its first beam at 0.15 mA. Electrons continue circulating rather than being lost after a few turns.
APS-U performs the world's first multi-bunch swap-out injection. With 12 bunches stored, the weakest is replaced every 30 seconds.
The septum magnet fails when its copper current bar ruptures after about a million pulses. This pulsed magnet directs incoming electrons into the ring. Beam operation resumes ten days later.
The ring stores 10 mA across many bunches. From 17 May, radiation from the beam removes gas from chamber walls in a process called vacuum conditioning.
Stored current reaches 25 mA, enough for beamline commissioning. The milestone is announced the next day.
Stored current reaches 50 mA.
The spare septum magnet develops a vacuum leak. The repaired original is reinstalled.
At 50 mA, X-rays first reach scientific beamline 27-ID for resonant inelastic X-ray scattering. The period dedicated to machine commissioning ends.
The upgraded APS is formally dedicated.

Measurements at 3-ID-B and 29-ID confirm the lowest emittance of any storage-ring light source at the time. Emittance, beam size multiplied by angular spread, is 45 pm·rad horizontally in flat mode and 28 pm·rad horizontally in round mode. The results are announced on 23 August.
Round-the-clock user experiments begin at 100 mA, with a 162-bunch mode and a 48-bunch timing mode.
The superconducting bunch-lengthening cavity is first used during user runs at 0.5 MV. By 2025 it operates at 1.1 MV with 200 mA stored.

Beam returns after the winter shutdown, and the first 2025 user run begins at 180 mA. The first half uses standard multi-bunch mode; the second uses timing mode. There are 27 beamlines accepting users and 43 in commissioning.
The ring reaches its 200 mA design current, twice the old current, and uses it for user operation.
Horizontal emittance is measured at about 33 pm·rad with 200 mA stored. The operating conditions are not stated.
HEXM at 20-ID measures its first sample. CHEX at 28-ID receives first light in all four branches, and sector 34 also receives first light.
Argonne holds a director's review of project delivery before DOE's CD-4 completion review.
DOE reviewers unanimously recommend project completion under Critical Decision 4, or CD-4, followed by close-out.
PtychoProbe at 33-ID and ATOMIC at 34-ID enter commissioning. All feature beamlines have reached commissioning or user operation, and 51 beamlines are accepting users.

After its first year of user operation, the new ring has delivered beam for 96.5% of scheduled hours. It runs at 200 mA in 216-bunch mode and 140 mA in 48-bunch timing mode. The beam is round and fully coupled, with a lifetime of 2 to 4 hours.
The PtychoProbe instrument is installed at 33-ID, the last feature beamline built by the project.
The project reports that all planned work has been delivered. DOE is reviewing formal completion, and the first 2026 user run is scheduled for 2 February.
DOE announces final approval of the APS Upgrade. The $815 million project delivered 9 new beamlines and 15 enhancements.
timeline.note: Exact CD-4 signature date not published. n20260205 says CD-4 'was granted following a two-day DOE review in late September 2025' and that DOE has since given final approval; a secondary source (HPCAT beamline page, via search summary only) dates final approval to January 2026. fdr1 Table 1.5 had planned CD-4 for 2nd quarter FY2026.

timeline.event: The APS begins replacing the klystron vacuum-tube amplifiers that power its radio-frequency cavities with solid-state amplifiers. Four are being installed for one sector's four cavities. Storage-ring conversion is expected by 2028, followed by the booster.
timeline.note: Wording corrected by verifier: the news item describes an installation in progress ('will power one sector'), not a completed changeover.

timeline.event: As of September 2026, the eight superconducting undulators planned for sectors 1, 11, 20 and 28 are delayed and not installed. Permanent-magnet devices remain in use there and at sector 6, where the 2019 design also specified a superconducting device.

exhibitNumbers.label: Speed of the electrons
exhibitNumbers.value: 99.9999996% of light speed, about 1.1 m/s slower than light
exhibitNumbers.explanation: At 6 GeV, an electron travels only about 1.1 m less than light in one second. Its energy is about 11,742 times its rest energy. This ratio is the Lorentz factor, γ = 6,000 MeV ÷ 0.511 MeV ≈ 11,742. The speed follows from 1 − v/c ≈ 1/(2γ²) = 3.6 × 10⁻⁹.

exhibitNumbers.label: Laps per second
exhibitNumbers.value: 271,647 laps around the 1.1 km ring each second
exhibitNumbers.explanation: The lap rate is light speed divided by the ring's circumference, f₀ = c ÷ C = 299,792,458 m/s ÷ 1,103.61 m. The electrons move slowly enough below light speed that the difference is negligible here. The radio-frequency system runs at exactly 1,296 times the lap rate, about 352 MHz.

exhibitNumbers.label: One lap
exhibitNumbers.value: 3.68 microseconds
exhibitNumbers.explanation: One lap takes 1 ÷ 271,647 of a second, or 3.68 microseconds. A microsecond is a millionth of a second. Each bunch of electrons sends a light pulse down each beamline once every 3.68 µs.

exhibitNumbers.label: Distance per day
exhibitNumbers.value: About 26 billion km per day, 173 times the Earth–Sun distance
exhibitNumbers.explanation: An electron circulating for a whole day would travel 271,647 laps/s × 1.1036 km × 86,400 s ≈ 2.59 × 10¹⁰ km. That is about 173 times the Earth–Sun distance of 1.496 × 10⁸ km, enough for more than 80 round trips. In practice, each bunch is replaced about every 72 minutes.

exhibitNumbers.label: Electrons in the ring
exhibitNumbers.value: 4.6 trillion electrons, carrying 736 nanocoulombs
exhibitNumbers.explanation: The beam current measures the charge passing a point each second. Each electron passes that point 271,647 times a second, so the stored charge is the current divided by the lap rate. At 0.2 A, this is 0.2 A ÷ 271,647 Hz = 736 nanocoulombs, or 4.6 × 10¹² electrons.

exhibitNumbers.label: Electrons in one bunch
exhibitNumbers.value: About 21 billion in 216-bunch mode, up to about 65 billion in 48-bunch timing mode
exhibitNumbers.explanation: In 216-bunch mode, each bunch carries 736 nC ÷ 216 = 3.4 nC, or 2.1 × 10¹⁰ electrons. In 48-bunch timing mode, each carries about 10 to 11 nC, or 6.2 to 6.7 × 10¹⁰ electrons. The injector limits timing-mode current to 130 to 140 mA. The 200 mA design would require 15.3 nC, or 9.6 × 10¹⁰ electrons, per bunch.
exhibitNumbers.source: derived; srp2024 Table 1 (9.6e10 electrons, 15.3 nC single bunch)

exhibitNumbers.label: Bunch spacing
exhibitNumbers.value: 17 ns in 216-bunch mode, 77 ns in timing mode
exhibitNumbers.explanation: The radio-frequency field creates 1,296 stable slots, called buckets, spaced 2.84 ns apart. Filling every sixth bucket gives 216 bunches at 17 ns intervals. This assumes even spacing; the exact fill pattern is not published. Filling every 27th bucket gives 48 bunches at 76.7 ns intervals. A nanosecond is a billionth of a second.

exhibitNumbers.label: Ring size
exhibitNumbers.value: 1,103.6 m around, about 350 m across, with 40 sectors
exhibitNumbers.explanation: The ring has 40 identical sectors, each 27.59 m long, for a circumference of 1,103.61 m. Rounded to 27.6 m per sector, this is about 1.1 km. A circle with that circumference would be about 351 m across. The actual ring consists of curved arcs joined by straight sections.

exhibitNumbers.label: A slightly smaller ring
exhibitNumbers.value: 38 cm shorter than the old ring
exhibitNumbers.explanation: The straight sections containing the undulators stayed in place, so their beamlines needed re-surveying and fine alignment. Fitting new arcs between these fixed points shortened the ring from 1,103.99 m to 1,103.61 m. Each bending-magnet source moved about 1.8 m upstream and 42 mm toward the ring's centre, requiring beamline realignment. The shorter path also raised the radio frequency by about 342 parts per million.

exhibitNumbers.label: Magnets
exhibitNumbers.value: 1,321 electromagnets, compared with 1,097 before the upgrade
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Each sector contains 33 magnets, and one extra corrector sits near injection. The total is 33 × 40 + 1 = 1,321, of 15 main types. Each sector has 7 forward bending magnets and 6 reverse bends, which are quadrupoles mounted off-centre to add a small backward bend. It also has 10 further quadrupoles to focus the beam, 6 sextupoles to correct focusing across electron energies, and 4 fast steering correctors. The old ring had 80 dipoles, 400 quadrupoles, 280 sextupoles, 317 correctors and 20 skew quadrupoles.

exhibitNumbers.label: Bending magnets per sector
exhibitNumbers.value: 7 forward and 6 reverse bends, replacing 2 forward bends
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Each sector turns the beam through a net 9°, or 360° ÷ 40. Seven forward bends spread this turn over more magnets, reducing the growth of the electron beam. Six small reverse bends change how electrons of different energies spread through the arc. They reduced the design emittance, the beam size multiplied by its angular spread, from 67 to 42 pm·rad.

exhibitNumbers.label: Total bending
exhibitNumbers.value: About 435° of bending per lap, with a net turn of 360°
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Some magnets bend the beam backward, so the forward bends must turn it through more than 360°. The forward turns total +397.8° and the backward turns −37.7°. Together they give about 435° of bending, while the net turn closes the ring at 360°.

exhibitNumbers.label: Magnet strength
exhibitNumbers.value: Quadrupole gradients of about 80 to 100 T/m, compared with about 20 T/m before
exhibitNumbers.explanation: A quadrupole's gradient measures how quickly its magnetic field increases away from the beam axis. A larger gradient provides stronger focusing. The new gradients are about 4 to 5 times the old value. They require bores about 26 mm across and pole tips made from vanadium permendur, a cobalt–iron alloy that supports stronger fields than ordinary magnet iron.

exhibitNumbers.label: Pre-built modules
exhibitNumbers.value: 200 modules, each up to about 6.5 m long and 27 tonnes
exhibitNumbers.explanation: The magnets were mounted and aligned on supports in an off-site workspace before the shutdown. Each module was carried into the tunnel on a Traksporter, placed within 25 mm of its final position, aligned to 1 mm and grouted to the floor. Each sector has five modules, named DLM-A, QMQ-A, FODO, QMQ-B and DLM-B. The central FODO module is the heaviest, about 27 tonnes over 6.3 m. The two DLM modules are the longest, about 6.5 m.
exhibitNumbers.source: fdr2 2-3.4.2; fdr5 5-3; ipac21 ('pre-assembled (in an off-site workspace) and eventually moved into the ring tunnel using Traksporters'); desy24 slide 8; apsNSR

exhibitNumbers.label: Installation pace
exhibitNumbers.value: About 1.2 modules per day
exhibitNumbers.explanation: All 200 magnet modules were installed between 12 July and 20 December 2023. Over those 162 days, installation averaged about 1.2 modules per calendar day.

exhibitNumbers.label: Alignment
exhibitNumbers.value: 15 µm rms within each module, against a 30 µm specification
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Within each module, magnets share a support and are aligned to 15 µm rms. Root-mean-square, or rms, measures the typical deviation from alignment. The specification was 30 µm. After installation, alignment between modules measured 50 µm horizontally and 35 µm vertically rms, within the ±100 µm specification around the 1.1 km ring.

exhibitNumbers.label: Vibration budget
exhibitNumbers.value: 10 nm rms for quadrupole vibration at 1 to 100 Hz
exhibitNumbers.explanation: The electron beam must stay steady to within 10% of its size. A moving quadrupole deflects the beam passing through it, so vibration between 1 and 100 cycles per second is limited to 10 nm rms. Root-mean-square, or rms, measures the typical vibration amplitude.

exhibitNumbers.label: Beam size at an undulator
exhibitNumbers.value: About 12 × 8 µm rms in round-beam user mode, compared with 275 × 10 µm before
exhibitNumbers.explanation: The zero-current model sizes are 12.3 × 8.3 µm rms in round-beam mode, or about 29 × 19 µm full width at half maximum. Root-mean-square, or rms, describes the width of the electron distribution. The old beam was 275 × 10 µm rms, roughly half a millimetre wide at half maximum. The flat-mode sizes are 14.5 × 3.1 µm rms, about 14 × 3 µm rounded. The cross-sectional area is about 27 to 62 times smaller than before, depending on mode.

exhibitNumbers.label: Emittance
exhibitNumbers.value: About 42 pm·rad natural emittance, compared with 3,100 pm·rad before; 28 to 44 pm·rad measured
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Emittance is beam size multiplied by angular spread, in picometre-radians. The natural, or model, value is 41.5 pm·rad, giving 3,100 ÷ 41.5 ≈ 75 times less than before. APS describes this as "almost a factor of 100". Measurements depend on coupling, the sharing of emittance between the two planes. They give 44 pm·rad horizontally in flat mode, or 28 horizontally and 31 vertically in round mode. The old vertical value was 40 pm·rad, so most of the round-mode improvement is horizontal.
exhibitNumbers.source: srp2024; ipac25 Table 1; fdr2 Table 2.1; sp2025
exhibitNumbers.note: Corrected by verifier: earlier text said the round-mode vertical emittance was 'not smaller than before'; 31 pm < 40 pm.

exhibitNumbers.label: Brightness
exhibitNumbers.value: About 500 times brighter; 100 to 1,000 times depending on X-ray energy
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Brightness measures photon output per source area, angular spread and narrow energy band. A smaller, more parallel source and twice the current give a design gain of ×540 at 20 keV for an undulator optimized for that energy. Other design estimates are roughly ×200 at 10 keV and ×600 to ×800 at 50 to 100 keV. Coherent flux gains are about ×160 at 10 keV and ×600 at 20 keV. These are calculations, not measured brightness gains.

exhibitNumbers.label: Vacuum chamber
exhibitNumbers.value: 22 mm wide, compared with a 42 × 85 mm chamber before; undulator chambers are 6.3 mm tall
exhibitNumbers.explanation: The 22 mm vacuum pipe leaves space for magnet poles close to the beam, supporting stronger focusing. Inside insertion devices, or undulators, the chamber is flattened to 6.3 mm tall with 0.6 mm walls. Most devices have an 8.5 mm design minimum magnet gap.
exhibitNumbers.source: fdr2 2-3.1; fdr3 Table 3.27; pac95; apsNSR ('an inch or less wide')

exhibitNumbers.label: Power radiated by the beam
exhibitNumbers.value: About 0.59 MW from bending magnets, up to about 0.9 MW with all undulators closed
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Each electron loses about 2.94 MeV as radiation in the bending magnets per lap in the as-built model; the 2019 design gave 2.87 MeV. At 0.2 A, this is 587 kW. Closing every undulator gap raises the loss to 4.47 MeV per lap, or 894 kW. Twelve radio-frequency cavities replace the lost energy on every lap.

exhibitNumbers.label: Energy stored in the beam
exhibitNumbers.value: 4.4 kilojoules
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Stored energy is charge multiplied by energy per unit charge, 736 nC × 6 GV = 4.42 kJ. For comparison, a 1,000 kg car moving at 2.97 m/s has the same kinetic energy, from ½mv², or about 3 m/s rounded. The beam concentrates this energy in a small cross-section. Before a full-beam dump, a fan-out kicker magnet spreads the bunches across the dump surface.

exhibitNumbers.label: Swap-out
exhibitNumbers.value: One depleted bunch is replaced about every 20 seconds
exhibitNumbers.explanation: The stable region in the new ring is too small to add electrons to stored bunches, so whole bunches are replaced during experiments. Kicker pulses about 11 ns long select one bunch without hitting neighbours 17 ns away. Each of the 216 bunches is renewed about every 72 minutes, from 216 × 20 s. With a beam lifetime of about 2 hours, it has then lost about 45% of its charge. A fresh bunch carries 5.4 to 6.1 nC, about 35 billion electrons.
exhibitNumbers.note: Corrected by verifier: the earlier text said a whole ~5-nC bunch is 'thrown out'; ~5 nC is the injected (BTS) charge, while the outgoing bunch carries much less.

exhibitNumbers.label: Superconducting harmonic cavity
exhibitNumbers.value: Niobium at 2.1 K, or −271 °C; bunches lengthen by a factor of 2 to 4
exhibitNumbers.explanation: The passing bunches excite the cavity at 1.4 GHz, four times the main radio frequency. The cavity has no external power source. Its electric field lengthens the bunches, reducing electron collisions that remove particles from the beam. In operation this roughly doubles the beam lifetime; the design expected a factor of four.

exhibitNumbers.label: Beam position monitors
exhibitNumbers.value: 560 pickups measure the beam position around the ring
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Fourteen pickups in each of 40 sectors measure the beam position so its orbit can be corrected. As of 2025, software corrections run up to 50 times per second. Fast orbit feedback with a 1 kHz bandwidth was removed from the project's scope and is being completed by the operating facility.

exhibitNumbers.label: Power supplies
exhibitNumbers.value: 2,247 power supplies
exhibitNumbers.explanation: There are 1,002 unipolar supplies, with current in one direction, and 921 slow bipolar supplies, with current in either direction. Another 322 are fast supplies. Two supplies each drive a string of bending magnets in series, one for all M1 bends and one for all M2 bends.

exhibitNumbers.label: Dark time
exhibitNumbers.value: 352 days from 24 April 2023 shutdown to 10 April 2024 commissioning; first beamline X-rays after 420 days
exhibitNumbers.explanation: The old ring was removed in 60 days. Crews then installed 200 magnet modules and assembled, tested and vacuum-baked the new ring. The first stored beam came 10 days into commissioning. X-rays first reached beamline 27-ID on 17 June 2024.

exhibitNumbers.label: Old ring removed
exhibitNumbers.value: About 1,900 tons planned for disposal or recycling, including about 200 girders of 6.8 to 11.3 tons each
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Some old magnets were retained for reuse. Jefferson Lab and Brookhaven National Laboratory received magnets for the Electron-Ion Collider project.

exhibitNumbers.label: Cost
exhibitNumbers.value: $815 million
exhibitNumbers.explanation: The US Department of Energy fixed the project cost in December 2018 when it approved the performance baseline, Critical Decision 2. Argonne reports that the upgrade was delivered within that budget.

exhibitNumbers.label: Users
exhibitNumbers.value: More than 5,500 scientists annually; 72 beamlines; 5,000 user hours per year
exhibitNumbers.explanation: The APS and partner institutions operate beamlines for materials science, chemistry, biology, geoscience and engineering. In its first year of user operation, the upgraded ring delivered beam for 96.5% of scheduled hours.

exhibitNumbers.label: Undulator precision
exhibitNumbers.value: 0.5 µm gap resolution, repeatability better than 3 µm; about 1 eV energy control at a 1 keV/s scan rate
exhibitNumbers.explanation: An undulator's magnet gap sets its X-ray energy. Reproducing the gap within micrometres keeps that energy accurate to about one electron-volt, even during scans at 1 keV per second.

exhibitNumbers.label: Beam height
exhibitNumbers.value: 1.40 m above the tunnel floor
exhibitNumbers.explanation: The 2019 Final Design Report specifies this height in its straight-section drawings. It places the electron beam roughly at adult chest height.

explainers.whatIsSynchrotron:
A synchrotron light source circulates electrons to produce light. At the APS, a linear accelerator, or linac, starts the electrons. A small accumulator ring gathers them into bunches, and a booster ring accelerates them to 6 billion electron-volts, or 6 GeV. At this energy they move at 99.9999996% of light speed. They circulate in a 1.1 km storage ring, where magnets bend their paths. The electrons emit radiation in a narrow forward cone as they bend.

The radiation spans infrared through hard X-rays. The APS uses the X-rays to study materials and biological samples. Undulators, rows of alternating magnets in 35 of the 40 straight sections, produce the brightest beams. Beamlines carry them to experiment stations. Twelve radio-frequency cavities replace the 2.9 to 4.5 MeV each electron loses per lap, depending on how many undulator gaps are closed. Replacing one depleted bunch about every 20 seconds keeps the current steady.
explainers.whatIsMBA:
Each of the APS ring's 40 sectors turns the electron beam through a net 9°. The old ring used two main bends per sector. Emitting photons changes the electrons' energies randomly, which contributes to beam spreading. A multi-bend achromat, or MBA, distributes the turn among more bends and uses focusing magnets between them. Theory predicts that emittance, beam size multiplied by angular spread, decreases roughly as the cube of the number of bends per sector. Changing from two to seven bends alone gives about a 40-fold reduction.

APS-U uses a hybrid seven-bend achromat based on the ESRF-EBS design at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility. The bending-magnet field decreases along each magnet. Six off-centre quadrupoles per sector add small reverse bends to control how electrons of different energies spread through the arc. These reduced the design emittance from about 67 to 42 picometre-radians, or pm·rad. With electron energy also reduced from 7 to 6 GeV, the change from the old ring is about 3,100 to 42 pm·rad. An achromat returns electrons with slightly different energies to the same path at the sector exit.
explainers.whyEmittanceMatters:
Emittance measures electron-beam size multiplied by angular spread. X-rays inherit both the source size and the spread of electron directions. A small, nearly parallel source can be focused to nanometre spots and remains narrow on the path to distant experiments. A smaller electron beam also increases the fraction of X-rays usable for coherent measurements.

APS-U reduced the horizontal emittance about 75-fold, from 3,100 to 42 pm·rad. Horizontal × vertical rms source sizes changed from about 275 × 10 µm to about 12 × 8 µm in round-beam user mode, or about 14 × 3 µm in flat mode. Root-mean-square, or rms, describes the electron distribution's width. This smaller source and twice the current give about 500 times greater brightness by design, with gains of 100 to 1,000 times depending on X-ray energy. The gain is greatest at high energies, where the old source was furthest from the diffraction limit. Near this limit, about wavelength divided by 4π in emittance, reducing the electron beam adds little.
explainers.whatIsCoherence:
Coherent light maintains a consistent relationship between its wave phases, so overlapping waves produce stable interference patterns. A laser is highly coherent; light from a bulb is much less so. For a fully coherent X-ray source, size multiplied by angular spread must be below about wavelength divided by 4π. This is roughly 10 pm·rad at 10 keV.

A larger source is partly coherent, so only a fraction of its photons is usable for coherent experiments. At 10 keV this was well below 0.1% at the old APS and is a few percent at APS-U. Better undulators and twice the current increase coherent flux further. Design gains are more than 100-fold, about 160 times at 10 keV and 600 times at 20 keV. Ptychography and coherent diffraction imaging reconstruct images from interference patterns called speckle. Their resolution depends on how far the scattered signal can be recorded. X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy, or XPCS, measures motion from changes in speckle, including motion of nanoparticles, polymer chains and magnetic domains.
explainers.whatIsUndulator:
An undulator has two rows of magnets with alternating north and south poles. Most APS devices are about 2.1 to 2.4 m long, with a magnetic pattern repeating every 1.35 to 3.3 cm. This repeat distance is the period. Electrons deflect from side to side about 60 to 175 times per pass. Radiation from these deflections reinforces at particular wavelengths, producing a narrow beam at a fundamental energy and its harmonics. The harmonics are higher-energy multiples of the fundamental. Opening or closing the magnet gap changes the field and tunes the X-ray energy. Most devices have an 8.5 mm design minimum gap, controlled with half-micrometre resolution. Sector 29 has a special electromagnetic device with a 12.5 cm period.

Superconducting undulators use wire coils cooled to −269 °C to produce stronger fields for high-energy X-rays. Eight are planned for APS-U. Sectors 1 and 20 each have an in-line pair with 16.5 mm periods and 1.9 m lengths. Sector 11 has two devices angled apart to feed independent beamlines, with 16.5 mm periods and 1.5 m lengths. Sector 28 has an angled pair with 18.5 mm periods and 1.2 to 1.3 m lengths. Manufacturing delays mean none was installed as of September 2026. Permanent-magnet devices are in use instead.
explainers.whatIsSwapOut:
The old APS added electrons to stored bunches every minute or two to maintain current. This top-up injection needed a large stable region around the stored beam. Stronger focusing leaves a stable region only about ±1.5 mm at the new injection point. APS-U therefore replaces whole depleted bunches with fresh ones from the booster.

A few hundred turns before a swap, a small decoherence kick spreads the outgoing bunch to prevent damage at the dump. Three fast kicker magnets then direct it into a shielded dump and place a fresh bunch in the same slot. Their pulses last about 11 ns, short enough to miss neighbouring bunches 17 ns away. In 2025 operation, one swap occurred about every 20 seconds, renewing each of 216 bunches roughly every 72 minutes. APS-U is the first storage-ring light source to operate this way.
explainers.whatIsBunchLengthening:
Electrons in dense bunches occasionally scatter off one another and leave the stored beam. This loss process is Touschek scattering. A superconducting niobium harmonic cavity lengthens the bunches to reduce their density without widening the beam. It operates at 2.1 K, or −271 °C. The passing bunches excite a field at four times the main radio frequency, lengthening them by a factor of 2 to 4.

At 1.1 MV and 200 mA, the cavity roughly doubles the beam lifetime in operation. The design expected about a fourfold increase. Longer bunches produce longer X-ray pulses. The design bunch lengths are about 88 to 104 ps rms, depending on fill pattern. A picosecond is a trillionth of a second; rms describes the width of the bunch distribution.
explainers.whyLowerEnergy:
APS-U reduced electron energy from 7 to 6 billion electron-volts, or GeV. For a fixed lattice, emittance grows with energy squared, so this reduction alone gives about 36% more brightness. Lower energy also allows weaker magnets for the same focusing. Radiation loss per lap scales with energy to the fourth power. Reducing that loss makes a 200 mA current, twice the old value, possible within the radio-frequency power capacity.

The tradeoff is lower photon energy, about 27% less for each undulator harmonic. Shorter-period undulators and higher harmonics compensate for this. Lower-energy bunches are also more sensitive to instabilities caused by their own electromagnetic fields and to collisions between their electrons.
explainers.whyRoundBeams:
APS-U usually shares emittance about equally between the horizontal and vertical planes. This is full coupling. Each plane measures about 28 to 31 pm·rad, producing a nearly round beam. Spreading electrons vertically lowers bunch density and reduces losses from Touschek scattering, collisions that remove electrons from the beam. The design used round beams as the default operating mode.

Flat mode has low coupling and emittances of about 40 × 4 pm·rad. Its smaller vertical source gives higher brightness but a shorter lifetime. It is workable with many bunches in the ring. In round mode, the measured vertical emittance of about 31 pm·rad is close to the old ring's 40 pm·rad. Most of the round-mode improvement is therefore horizontal.
explainers.whyLowerEnergy_source: fdr2 2-1.3 (Choice of Beam Energy): emittance scales quadratically with energy (36% brightness gain), lower energy is more susceptible to wakefield instabilities, IBS and Touschek loss, magnet gradients scale with energy, and radiated power scales as E^4.
explainers.whyRoundBeams_source: ler25 slide 20; ipac25 Table 1; srp2024 (text and Table 5); fdr2 2-2.3 / Table 2.13 ('default round-beam modes'; flat-beam lifetime shorter)
explainers.whatIsSwapOut_note: +/-1.5 mm is the measured horizontal aperture at the injection point including the septum limit (ler25 slide 13).
